params.question: In the clinical scenario described, the pregnant woman's husband cannot be a carrier of the cystic fibrosis gene because he is healthy and shows no symptoms.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is false. As the narration explained, a recessive allele can hide silently for generations without causing symptoms. Carriers of autosomal recessive conditions are healthy. Since the husband's sister had cystic fibrosis, both his parents are likely carriers, meaning the husband himself has a significant chance of carrying the same mutation.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Well done. Carriers of autosomal recessive conditions are typically healthy and show no symptoms at all. Since the husband's sister had cystic fibrosis, both his parents are likely carriers, giving the husband a significant probability of carrying the CFTR mutation despite being completely well.

params.question: Why does consanguinity increase the risk of autosomal recessive disorders, as explained in this section?

answers.text: Related couples are more likely to both carry the same rare recessive allele inherited from a shared ancestor

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Consanguineous partners descend from a common ancestor and are therefore more likely to both carry the same rare recessive allele, increasing the chance that their child will be homozygous and affected.

answers.text: Marriage between relatives introduces new dominant mutations through inbreeding

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Consanguinity does not create new mutations. It increases the probability that both parents carry the same pre-existing recessive allele from their shared lineage.

answers.text: Related parents always have identical genotypes, guaranteeing that every child will be affected

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Related parents share more alleles than unrelated parents, but their genotypes are not identical. The risk of an affected child is increased, not guaranteed.

answers.text: Consanguinity only increases the risk of X-linked conditions, not autosomal recessive ones

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Consanguinity primarily raises the risk of autosomal recessive conditions because both parents are more likely to carry the same rare recessive allele. The effect on X-linked conditions is much less significant.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the section on consanguinity. The key point is that related partners share segments of DNA from a common ancestor, making it more likely that both carry the same rare recessive mutation.
Well done. This mechanism is clinically important in India, where uncle-niece and first-cousin marriages remain common in several communities, making rare recessive disorders more prevalent.

params.question: According to Falconer's threshold model described in this section, why do first-degree relatives of an affected person have a higher recurrence risk for multifactorial diseases?

answers.text: They inherit the exact same set of causative alleles, giving them identical disease liability

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. First-degree relatives share approximately 50% of their genes, not all of them. Their liability is shifted towards the threshold but is not identical to the affected person's.

answers.text: They share approximately half their genes with the affected person, shifting their liability distribution closer to the disease threshold

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Sharing about 50% of genes moves the liability curve of first-degree relatives closer to the threshold, resulting in a recurrence risk of roughly 2–10% — higher than the general population but far lower than the 25–50% seen in single-gene Mendelian conditions.

answers.text: Multifactorial diseases follow a fixed Mendelian ratio of 25% in first-degree relatives

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. A hallmark of multifactorial inheritance is that it does not follow fixed Mendelian ratios. The recurrence risk is typically 2–10%, not 25%.

answers.text: First-degree relatives are always exposed to the same environmental triggers as the affected person

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. While family members may share some environmental exposures, partial gene-sharing is the primary reason their liability is shifted. Environmental factors contribute but do not fully explain familial clustering.

overallFeedback.feedback: Revisit Falconer's threshold model. The key insight is that first-degree relatives share roughly half their genetic liability, placing their distribution closer to the disease threshold than the general population.

Excellent. Understanding the threshold model helps explain why conditions like neural tube defects, type 2 diabetes, and coronary artery disease cluster in families without following clean Mendelian patterns.

params.question: In the clinical vignette, a four-year-old girl from Hyderabad has bowed legs despite normal vitamin D intake, and her father also has bowed legs. Genetic testing reveals a PHEX gene mutation. Which inheritance pattern does this illustrate?

answers.text: Autosomal recessive — both parents must carry the mutation for the child to be affected

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. In autosomal recessive inheritance, both parents are typically unaffected carriers. Here the father himself is affected, and the PHEX gene is located on the X chromosome, not an autosome.

answers.text: Autosomal dominant — a single copy on an autosome causes the condition in every generation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Although the condition does appear in consecutive generations like an autosomal dominant trait, PHEX is on the X chromosome, not an autosome. The key clue is that fathers pass their X chromosome to all daughters.

answers.text: X-linked dominant — the father passed his X chromosome carrying the mutant PHEX gene to his daughter

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Fathers pass their single X chromosome to all daughters and their Y chromosome to all sons. Since PHEX is on the X, every daughter of an affected father inherits the mutation, making this X-linked dominant inheritance.

answers.text: Mitochondrial — the condition was inherited through maternal cytoplasm

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. In mitochondrial inheritance, the condition is passed only from the mother to all children. Here the affected parent is the father, and PHEX is a nuclear gene, not a mitochondrial one.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the father-to-daughter transmission described in the vignette. The PHEX gene is on the X chromosome, and fathers pass their X to every daughter — this is the hallmark of X-linked dominant inheritance.
Well done. Vitamin D-resistant rickets (X-linked hypophosphataemia) is a classic example of X-linked dominant inheritance, where affected fathers transmit the condition to all daughters but no sons.
